title: One leaf in the pot
hook: Krishna eats one leaf from Draupadi's empty pot and ten thousand hungry sages feel full; why food goes to God first and comes back as prasad
carry: when god is fed, everyone is fed
tomorrow: The paste meant for a king

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water, and the river Shiva caught in his hair. Your line was the Ganga came down to purify. Today, the sweet on the plate, and an empty pot.
screen: `THE WATER — THE GANGA CAME DOWN TO PURIFY.`

segments.voice: The Pandavas are living in exile in the forest, and they have one treasure: a pot from the Sun god that gives food every day, until Draupadi has eaten. Then it's empty till morning. Their cousin Duryodhana knows this. So he sends them a guest: the sage Durvasa, famous for his temper, with ten thousand disciples, timed to arrive just after Draupadi has finished her meal. Durvasa says: we'll bathe in the river, then we eat. Draupadi looks at the empty pot. If she can't feed them, the curse will be terrible. So she closes her eyes and calls Krishna.
screen: `A POT THAT FEEDS THEM DAILY.` → `UNTIL DRAUPADI EATS.` → `TEN THOUSAND HUNGRY GUESTS.` → `SHE CALLS KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Krishna appears, and the first thing he says is: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat. Draupadi almost cries: there's nothing, that's the whole problem. Bring the pot, he says. Stuck to the rim is one tiny leaf of cooked greens. Krishna eats it, and says: may the one who is the soul of the whole world be satisfied. Down at the river, ten thousand sages suddenly feel completely full. They're too embarrassed to come back, and they slip away. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. Here's the teaching. Krishna's line names it: God is the soul in every being, so feeding God is never feeding just one. An old Hindu picture puts it simply: water the root of a tree, and every branch is fed. That's naivedya, today's word: food offered to God before anyone eats. The cook often doesn't taste it while cooking, because the first taste isn't theirs. A little goes before the image on a clean plate, sometimes with a tulsi leaf on top, and sits for a few moments. Then the plate comes back, and it isn't just food anymore. It's prasad, grace, and it's shared with everyone: the family, the guest at the door, the neighbor. People take it in the right hand, often with a small bow, and try not to refuse it. Feed God first, and the food comes back for all. That's why the laddus wait.
screen: `ONE LEAF ON THE RIM.` · `TEN THOUSAND SAGES FEEL FULL.` · `NAIVEDYA: GOD EATS FIRST.` · `PRASAD: IT COMES BACK FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Set something small to eat in front of you, a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a few raisins, and pause before you eat it. If you pray, offer it first, to Krishna or a name you honor, and wait a few breaths before you take it back as prasad. If you don't pray, hold it as a gift you didn't make by yourself: the sun, the farmer, the driver. Then break it in two if you can, put half aside for someone else, and eat your half slowly.
Naivedya. Food offered to God before anyone eats, which comes back as prasad for everyone, like one leaf that fed ten thousand.
Your line: when God is fed, everyone is fed. One leaf from an empty pot. See you tomorrow.

screen: `WHEN GOD IS FED, EVERYONE IS FED.` → `DAY 116 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PASTE MEANT FOR A KING.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus place a small portion of food, often a sweet or fruit, before the image at the home shrine as naivedya, wait a few moments, and then receive it back as prasad, grace, sharing it with everyone in the house and any guests.

what a scholar hears: the Durvasa episode (the akshaya patra and Krishna's single leaf) belongs to the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata's vulgate and is absent from the critical edition; the root-and-branches image is Bhagavata Purana 4.31.14; naivedya is one of the standard services of puja.
